newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Treasury seen pushing for Australia rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Treasury seen pushing for Australia rate cut.

text.p: Australian Treasury Secretary Ted Evans, the government's representative on the board of the Reserve Bank, argued on Tuesday that wages growth was not accelerating and economic growth could be boosted.
Economists said the comments suggested Evans would argue for another interest rate cut at the Reserve Bank's next board meeting on June 3.

Speaking after the release of data showing private sector wages growth accelerated to 1.3 percent in the three months to end-February from 0.8 percent in the previous three months, Evans said recent wages data did not threaten his forecast of two percent annual underlying inflation.

He told an economists' luncheon that private sector wages data was so flawed it was simply not believable and that wages growth was closer to the 1.0 percent figure shown for all sectors wages growth in the three months to February 28.

"The best one could draw out of those figures is that we've been running at one percent a quarter for some time, including going back through to that low March quarter of last year, so it's doubtful that's there's been an acceleration as such," Evans said.

The Reserve Bank warned as recently as two weeks ago that wages growth was uncomfortably high and that if it accelerated any further, the bank would raise interest rates to keep underlying inflation in its targeted two to three percent band.

Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane, seen as more hawkish than the government and Treasurer, said two weeks ago that there would be no economic gain in another rate cut and that wages growth was uncomfortably high given the inflation outlook.
However, Evans made clear that he saw few wages threats to inflation and also said growth could be boosted to reduce unemployment, if that was what policy-makers wanted.
"I'm prepared to believe that we can grow at a considerably faster rate than three-and-a-half percent if we want, in fact I know we can," Evans said.
Economists who were present at the luncheon said his comments showed he was likely to favour a fourth interest rate cut in this cycle. Official cash rates are now six percent.
"I walked away from that thinking he would argue for a rate cut," said Citibank chief economist Stephen Koukoulas.
"Whether it will be enough to convince the other board members remains to be seen," he said.

Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson said Evans made a number of points which left the way open for an interest rate cut, including his comments on the benign inflation outlook and the steady wages growth.

"If anything, since the last board meeting there are more clouds over the strength of the economy and it does seem to point to a better than even chance that they'll cut again at the next meeting," Henderson said. "I don't think Ted Evans is going to be arguing against it," he said.

Evans was rumoured to have argued for a rate cut at the last board meeting on May 6, but was thought to have been voted down by board members led by Macfarlane arguing that the wages outlook was still too dangerous.
Evans said he would not comment on the speculation.
The board now appears likely to face another rate cut battle at its June meeting, economists said.
